newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street Journal told to change name of section.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street Journal told to change name of section.

text.p: A California judge issued a preliminary injunction on Thursday barring The Wall Street Journal from calling a weekly section "California Journal" after a magazine of that name sued the newspaper's publisher.

The magazine, a Sacramento-based monthly of state politics founded in 1970, sued when the business daily announced plans to include a weekly section of state business news, dubbed "California Journal," in its California editions.
After the first installment appeared on Oct. 2, California Journal said in a statement that the newspaper was trying to steal its name.

A hearing in the suit was held on Tuesday. On Thursday Sacramento Superior Court Judge Earl Warren Jr. granted a preliminary injunction forbidding Dow Jones & Co. Inc., publishers of The Wall Street Journal, from using "California Journal" as a title in any section or pages of any publications pending a trial and final ruling in the case.

"We're very excited. At the moment we're feeling like David who just felled the giant," said Tom Hoeber, publisher of the California Journal, which has a circulation of 15,000, compared with The Wall Street Journal's 1.9 million.
Hoeber said the case could take several months to go to trial.
Neither a lawyer nor a spokesman for Dow Jones & Co. could immediately be reached for comment.

Warren, son of the former U.S. chief justice, said in his written ruling that the California Journal was "likely to prevail on the merits of its common law trademark infringement and unfair competition claim."

He said the evidence established that the California Journal had a "protectable interest" in the exclusive use of its name. Warren said the public had come to associate the name with the monthly magazine and The Wall Street Journal's use of it "creates a likelihood of confusion in the consuming public as to the source of the news and analysis."
He said The Wall Street Journal could continue publishing its feature if it called it something else.
